Tax Administration is on the third floor at 201 East Main Street, Durham, and answers at 919-560-0300. Appeals, bills and relief applications all start there, and the Land Records team works from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM.

An online Tax Help portal lets owners file an appeal, message staff and follow the status of a case. To pay, go to pay.dconc.gov, mail a check to the Tax Collector at P.O. Box 580240, Charlotte, NC 28258-0240, pay at the counter, or pay by phone (a convenience fee applies). E-check adds a $3.25 processing fee.

Inside the city you pay both a county and a city tax, so look at both bills when you plan a sale.

Durham County had an estimated 347,240 residents in July 2025, 6.9% above the 2020 estimates base, with 164,222 housing units. Owners occupy just 55.5% of homes, which leaves a large rental segment. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $389,400, median gross rent is $1,508, and median household income is $82,316. Builders pulled 4,772 permits in 2025.

The Board of County Commissioners approved a countywide rate of 57.92 cents per $100 of property value in the 2026-2027 budget ordinance. The City of Durham kept its rate at 43.71 cents per $100 for the same year.

  • Durham County: 57.92 cents per $100 for 2026-27.
  • City of Durham: 43.71 cents per $100 for 2026-27.
  • Owners of residential property in unincorporated Durham County get a solid waste decal with the mailed bill.

The 2025 reappraisal reshaped the rate history. Total taxable value grew from $43 billion in 2019 to more than $70 billion. The county rate fell from 0.7987 to a revenue-neutral 0.5192, and the rate set for 2025-26 was 0.5542. For 2026-27 it is 57.92 cents.

Bills come due September 1, and you have until January 5 to pay without penalty. Until then you can also make partial payments on real property with no interest or added cost.

Pay as soon as the bill arrives, or send it to the escrow department if your lender pays it. Under the state schedule, January 6 begins a 2% charge, and each month or fraction after February 1 adds three-fourths of a percent.

The statutory lien on a parcel dates from January 1, the listing date, and carries any penalties, interest and costs. A sale later in the year does not remove it. Only payment does.

If you are selling in the fall, remember that the bill follows the parcel and the closing attorney will want the amount owed in writing. Call 919-560-0300 for it, and check whether the e-check fee of $3.25 or the phone convenience fee matters to you when you pick how to pay. A check by mail to the Charlotte P.O. box is the plain option, but allow time for it to arrive before January 5.

The tax office can look only at appraised value. Tax rates, affordability and services are outside an appeal. If you believe the value is well above or below what the property would have sold for on January 1, 2025, you can appeal.

The Board of Equalization and Review can still allow a late application until December 31, and owners who miss a deadline are advised to apply in future years. Appeals on personal property and vehicles generally run on a 30 day clock from the bill, or from a separate value notice if one was sent.

Useful evidence:

  • An independent appraisal based on comparable sales near the reappraisal date.
  • The deed and related appraisal information.
  • A list of comparable sales from the same period.
  • Surveys, plat maps and photographs, especially of condition problems.

The path has three levels. An informal review with a staff appraiser typically takes 30 to 120 days, and any agreed value is only a recommendation. The Board of Equalization and Review, appointed by the commissioners, makes it final, and attendance is optional. Proof is the taxpayer's job. Beyond that, a petition to the NC Property Tax Commission must go in within 30 days of the board's mailed decision.

Durham publishes three state homestead programs plus one local program. The state programs share a June 1 filing date. The elderly and disabled exclusion takes a single application, while the circuit breaker is renewed every year.

Homeowner tax relief programs in Durham County
ProgramWhat it doesMain requirement
Elderly/Disabled Homestead ExemptionRemoves $25,000 or half of assessed value, whichever is greater, for the home and up to 1 acreAge 65 or older, or totally and permanently disabled, with 2025 income of $38,800 or less
Circuit Breaker defermentLimits tax to 4% of income, or 5% in the higher tier; the excess is deferredSame age and disability rules, income up to $58,250, and five years of ownership and residence
Disabled Veteran ExclusionRemoves the first $45,000 of appraised valueTotal and permanent service-connected disability; open regardless of age or income
DSS Low Income Homeowner ReliefHelp toward the current bill through a three-tier income modelHousehold at or below 80% of area median income, five or more years in the home, apply through DSS

DSS applications open each September 1, and that program cannot be combined with the homestead exclusion. A circuit breaker owner who sells owes the deferred taxes for the most recent 3 years at transfer, with interest.

Ask Tax Administration for a payoff figure before closing so the year's bill is settled at the table. A sale can also bring an appraiser to the property, and a structure built after 2025 is valued using January 1, 2025 market rates.

  • The seller buys the state deed stamp at the register of deeds, a dollar for each five hundred dollars of price, before recording.
  • Assessed value stays tied to the January 1, 2025 market, so a newer sale price can differ from it.
  • Owners with a deferred circuit breaker balance should request the figure early.

An inherited or tenant-occupied house with a long tax history needs the same payoff request. The relief team can say whether an exclusion should have been on the account.

A cash buyer can close quickly, which helps when a bill is close to January 5 and penalties are coming. A cash sale also skips a lender's appraisal and underwriting. The tax payoff, the deed stamp and recording costs are still due at the closing table.

faqs.q: What is the Durham County property tax rate?
faqs.a: The countywide rate for 2026-27 is 57.92 cents per $100 of property value. Owners inside the city also pay the City of Durham rate of 43.71 cents per $100.

faqs.q: When are Durham County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Each September 1, with no penalty until after January 5. Partial payments on real property are allowed until then.

faqs.q: Can I still appeal my Durham County property value?
faqs.a: The Board of Equalization and Review can allow a late application until December 31, and you can apply again in future years. Call 919-560-0300 to find out what the board will accept.

faqs.q: How do I apply for Durham County tax relief?
faqs.a: Apply to the county assessor by June 1 on Form AV-9 for the elderly or disabled exclusion or the circuit breaker, adding the NCDVA-9 form for the disabled veteran exclusion. Call 919-560-0300 for help with the form.

faqs.q: Who buys the deed stamp on a Durham County sale?
faqs.a: The seller. The state rate is a dollar per five hundred dollars of price, paid to the register of deeds before recording.
